theme: Event calendars: FIFA World Cup 2026 schedule and host-city data, Olympics, concerts (Setlist.fm, Songkick, Ticketmaster API), conferences, PredictHQ samples, holiday calendars by country

candidates.name: openfootball/world-cup.json
candidates.what_it_holds: Match schedules (dates, kickoff times, teams, venues, group assignments, scores) for FIFA World Cups from 1930 through 2026, organized in year-labeled JSON files; description explicitly lists 'Canada/USA/Mexico 2026'. Public-domain dedication, files fetchable directly via raw GitHub URLs (no API key), so the 2026 match calendar (dates and host cities, June-July 2026, inside 3Q26) can be pulled as a one-command JSON fetch.
candidates.why_useful: Directly fills gap #11 (FIFA World Cup 2026 schedule/host-city data) with the exact match dates/venues needed to build a 3Q26 host-city demand-shock calendar for the North America nights forecast.
candidates.last_activity: not confirmed exact date; actively maintained per description

candidates.name: jfjelstul/worldcup (Fjelstul World Cup Database)
candidates.what_it_holds: 27 linked datasets (>1.5M data points) on tournaments, teams, players, managers, referees, stadiums, matches, goals, bookings for all 22 men's World Cups (1930-2022) and 9 women's World Cups (1991-2019); available as R package, .RData, .csv, .json, and SQLite.
candidates.why_useful: Deep historical World Cup base-rate data (host-city attendance/stadium capacity patterns) useful for calibrating how prior World Cups moved host-country travel/lodging demand, though it stops at 2022 and does not itself cover 2026.

candidates.name: vacanza/holidays (Python `holidays` package)
candidates.what_it_holds: Python library computing government-designated public/bank/school/religious holidays on the fly for 250 country codes plus subdivisions (states/provinces) and 20+ financial-market calendars (ISO 10383 MICs); not a static file but a deterministic calendar engine, multi-language holiday names, ~4,066 commits, MIT license, 1.9k stars.
candidates.why_useful: Gives a machine-pullable, per-country/per-subdivision holiday calendar (long weekends, school holidays) to build controls for seasonality and demand shocks in the nights/ADR forecast across all ABNB regions (NA/EMEA/LatAm/APAC), addressing the 'holiday calendars by country' part of gap #11.
candidates.time_coverage: computed for any year, historical and future

candidates.name: nager/Nager.Date
candidates.what_it_holds: Public-holiday library/API (.NET, NuGet, Docker) plus a free public REST API (nagerholidays.com) returning JSON holiday records (date, local/English name, country code, subdivision, holiday type) for 200+ countries; 1,706 commits, MIT license.
candidates.why_useful: Alternative/cross-check source to the Python `holidays` package for per-country holiday calendars, reachable via a plain HTTP GET with no auth for a quick one-off pull (e.g. from a notebook without pandas/holidays installed).
candidates.license: MIT (API free tier; some offline packages need a sponsor key)
candidates.last_activity: not confirmed exact date; actively maintained

candidates.name: peopledoc/workalendar
candidates.what_it_holds: Python module computing legal/religious holidays and working-day arithmetic for 80+ countries/territories including US state-level, Canada, Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Chile, China, Japan, Korea, India, Australia, NZ, South Africa and more; includes precomputed astronomical data (equinoxes, solar terms) for 1991-2051; MIT license, ~1,377 commits, 950 stars.
candidates.why_useful: Second independent holiday/working-day calendar engine with stronger LatAm/APAC subdivision coverage than some alternatives, useful for regional (LatAm/APAC) seasonality controls referenced in gap #11 and cross-checking the `holidays` package.
candidates.time_coverage: 1991-2051 for astronomical holidays; general holiday rules for any year

candidates.name: tech-conferences/conference-data (confs.tech backing data)
candidates.what_it_holds: JSON files (one per topic/year) of tech conferences worldwide with fields for name, start/end dates, city/country location, CFP dates, social handles; 13,987 commits, community-maintained, MIT license, covers many years across dozens of tech topics (JS, Python, Rust, data, etc.).
candidates.why_useful: A machine-readable conference calendar with dates and host cities that can proxy business-travel demand spikes in specific ABNB markets (partial coverage of the 'conferences' part of gap #11); skewed toward software/tech conferences only, not a general conference census.
candidates.last_activity: actively maintained (19 open PRs, 4 open issues at capture)

candidates.name: predicthq/sdk-py
candidates.what_it_holds: Official PredictHQ Python API client (341 commits, MIT license) exposing endpoints for events, broadcasts, places, features, and demand 'impact' analysis; requires a PredictHQ access_token (paid API), so it is a pull method rather than committed data.
candidates.why_useful: Would be the mechanical route to a global events-and-impact feed (concerts, conferences, sports, public holidays, severe weather) PredictHQ sells, matching the 'PredictHQ samples' keyword in the theme, but is gated behind a paid API key that the project rules say not to use (no paid keys) — catalogued as a method only, not actionable without a licence.
candidates.time_coverage: current + historical via API, subject to plan
candidates.license: MIT (client code); underlying data is a paid product

candidates.name: predicthq/phq-data-science-docs
candidates.what_it_holds: PredictHQ data-science documentation with downloadable Jupyter notebooks illustrating academic-calendar events, demand forecasting, severe weather, live-TV events and venue-data use cases via the (paid) PredictHQ API; 286 commits, MIT license; no committed raw CSV datasets found.
candidates.why_useful: Shows worked examples of how an events-impact feed could be joined to demand series (methodological reference for building our own event-shock feature even if we don't buy PredictHQ), but supplies no standalone data.

candidates.name: rgriff23/Olympic_history
candidates.what_it_holds: R scripts and compiled tabular data of Olympic athlete/event history 1896-2016, scraped from sports-reference.com; underlies the well-known Kaggle '120 years of Olympic history' dataset.
candidates.why_useful: Historical Olympics host-city/year reference (useful for base-rating how past Games moved host-city travel demand), but athlete/medal-level detail is not directly a travel-demand series and the dataset stops at 2016 (does not cover Tokyo 2020, Paris 2024, or Milano-Cortina 2026).
candidates.license: not confirmed (data originally scraped, redistributed for research use)

candidates.name: GDELT ecosystem (e.g. gdeltPyR, gdeltr2, spark-gdelt)
candidates.what_it_holds: 145 public repos tagged 'gdelt'; gdeltPyR (257 stars) is a Python client to pull GDELT 1.0/2.0 global event/news-tone data; gdeltr2 is the R equivalent; spark-gdelt runs GDELT through Apache Spark for large-scale event/news processing. All are acquisition tools over GDELT's own public data lake, not committed datasets.
candidates.why_useful: GDELT already flagged in CONTEXT gap #14 (text/social); these are the concrete, actively used client libraries (gdeltPyR in particular) that make a GDELT pull mechanical for a global news/event-tone or shock-detection feature (e.g. World Cup/conference/regulatory news spikes by country).
candidates.time_coverage: GDELT 1.0 (1979-) / 2.0 (2015-) as hosted by GDELT project
candidates.license: varies by repo (gdeltPyR: MIT-style, check repo)
candidates.last_activity: gdeltPyR last significant activity years ago per star history; topic page shows repos updated through 2026

notes: WebSearch tool returned 'session has used its web search budget (200 of 200)' on the very first call for this scout — every actual query had to be run through WebFetch against specific GitHub URLs (direct guesses, github.com/topics/<tag> listing pages, and a github.com/search?q=... page) instead of true web search, so coverage of the concert/ticketing side (Setlist.fm/Songkick/Ticketmaster) is weaker than the calendar/World Cup side: the topic pages for setlist-fm, songkick, and ticketmaster-api surfaced mostly personal hobby projects (Spotify-playlist generators, Telegram bots, Chrome extensions) with no committed datasets worth flagging, and specific client-repo name guesses (ticketpy, setlist-fm-api-client, predicthq client-python) 404'd. One github.com/search?q=... call hit a 429 rate limit (Retry-After 3600s), so a broader 'world cup 2026 host city venues' repo search could not be completed — worth another scout revisiting that specific query later. Best finds: openfootball/world-cup.json (has an actual 2026 schedule file, public domain) and the holidays/workalendar/Nager.Date trio for the 'holiday calendars by country' sub-theme. Olympics and Ticketmaster/Songkick/Setlist.fm concert data on GitHub skew toward personal/hobby integrations with no reusable datasets; PredictHQ itself is API-only and paid, so only cataloged as a method, consistent with the 'no paid keys' rule.
